samples.text:
The three pie charts shows where adults in one country got their news in 2005, 2015 and 2025.

In 2005, television was the most popular source with 48%. Newspapers was second with 27%, radio was 13% and news websites was 10%. Social media was very small with only 2%.

In 2015, television was still first but it fell to 40%. Newspapers dropped a lot to 14% and radio also fell to 10%. On the other hand, news websites increased to 22% and social media also increased to 14%, so it was same as newspapers.

In 2025, social media became the most popular source, it was 36%. Television decreased again to 29%. News websites was nearly same with 21%. Newspapers and radio fell down more, to only 6% and 8%.

Overall, the traditional sources like television, newspapers and radio become less popular during the twenty years, but social media and news websites grew a lot, and social media was the number one source in 2025.
samples.why: All three charts described with accurate figures · overview present but placed last · year-by-year structure is mechanical · limited range of vocabulary and linking · several agreement, article and tense errors.

samples.text:
The pie charts illustrate the main sources of news used by adults in one country in 2005, 2015 and 2025.

Overall, traditional media such as television, newspapers and radio became steadily less popular over the twenty-year period, while online sources grew. Most notably, social media rose from being the least used source to the most popular.

In 2005, almost half of adults (48%) relied mainly on television for news, and newspapers were the second most common source, at 27%. Radio and news websites accounted for 13% and 10% respectively, while only 2% of people used social media.

Ten years later, the share of television had dropped to 40%, and the figure for newspapers had almost halved, to 14%. News websites, however, more than doubled to 22%, and social media also expanded rapidly to 14%. By 2025, social media had become the leading source of news, at 36%, overtaking television, which fell to 29%. News websites remained stable at 21%, whereas newspapers and radio continued to decline, reaching just 6% and 8%.
samples.why: Clear overview of the main trends across three charts · key features highlighted with accurate figures and correct derived comparisons · logical progression · range of cohesive devices · few errors.

samples.text:
The charts compare the main sources from which adults in one country obtained their news at three points between 2005 and 2025.

Over the two decades, there was a pronounced shift from traditional to digital media. Television, newspapers and radio all lost popularity, while social media grew from a negligible share to become the leading source of news.

In 2005, television was clearly dominant, used by 48% of adults, and newspapers were a strong second at 27%. Radio (13%) and news websites (10%) played a smaller role, and social media was used by a mere 2%.

By 2015, the balance was beginning to change. Television's share had eroded to 40%, and newspapers had lost roughly half of their audience share, falling to 14%. At the same time, news websites more than doubled to 22%, and social media drew level with newspapers at 14%. The following decade saw this shift accelerate: social media surged to 36%, eighteen times its 2005 figure, overtaking television, which slipped to 29%. News websites held steady at 21%, whereas newspapers dwindled to just 6%, less than a quarter of their original share, and radio fell to 8%.
samples.why: Key trends skilfully selected across three charts · clear, well-placed overview · accurate figures and derived comparisons used purposefully · seamless cohesion · precise vocabulary (eroded, dwindled) · wide range of error-free structures.
